rubric.why: Reduction can be defined by electron transfer or by the corresponding oxygen/hydrogen change.
rubric.description: States a correct definition of reduction.
rubric.how: Award for any one valid definition of reduction.

rubric.why: Identifies the process as reduction rather than merely naming a related reaction.
rubric.description: Clearly identifies the stated change as reduction.
rubric.how: Award when the definition explicitly names reduction.

modelAnswer: Reduction is the gain of electrons by an atom, ion or molecule.
It may also be described as removal of oxygen or addition of hydrogen.

items.followUp: What is a strong electrolyte? Give one example.

rubric.why: Weak electrolytes ionize only partially in solution; weak acids and weak bases are examples.
rubric.description: Identifies weak electrolytes as partially ionizing substances or as weak acids and bases.
rubric.how: Award for stating partial ionization or identifying weak acids/bases.

rubric.why: These are standard examples of weak electrolytes.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example of a weak electrolyte.
rubric.how: Award for at least one correct example.

modelAnswer: Weak electrolytes ionize only partially in water.
Weak acids and weak bases are weak electrolytes; examples include acetic acid (CH₃COOH) and ammonium hydroxide (NH₄OH).

rubric.why: An oxidizing agent accepts electrons from another substance.
rubric.description: States that an oxidizing agent accepts electrons.
rubric.how: Award for electron acceptance or gain.

rubric.why: The oxidizing agent causes oxidation of another substance and is itself reduced.
rubric.description: States the effect on the other substance or the agent's own change.
rubric.how: Award for either correct relationship.

modelAnswer: An oxidizing agent is a substance that accepts electrons from another substance.
It causes oxidation of that substance and is itself reduced.

items.followUp: Describe the conclusions of the alpha-particle scattering experiment.

rubric.why: The experiment directed alpha particles at thin gold foil and detected them with a fluorescent screen.
rubric.description: Describes the essential experimental arrangement.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the alpha particles and gold foil, or the detecting screen.

rubric.why: Most alpha particles passed through the foil without deflection.
rubric.description: States the observation that most particles passed through undeflected.
rubric.how: Award for the observation.

rubric.why: A small number were deflected, and very few were reflected backwards.
rubric.description: States the unusual deflections or backscattering.
rubric.how: Award for either deflection or backward reflection.

rubric.why: The observations showed that most of the atom is empty space and that its positive charge is concentrated in a very small nucleus.
rubric.description: Gives the empty-space conclusion and/or the small positive nucleus conclusion.
rubric.how: Award for a correct conclusion about empty space or the small, positively charged nucleus.

rubric.why: Rutherford's model placed electrons around the central nucleus; the atom as a whole is neutral.
rubric.description: Describes electrons around the nucleus or the neutral atom.
rubric.how: Award for the electron arrangement or overall neutrality.

modelAnswer: Rutherford directed alpha particles from a radioactive source at a very thin gold foil and detected them with a fluorescent screen.
Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil without deflection.
Some particles were deflected, and a very few bounced back.
He concluded that most of an atom is empty space and that its positive charge and most of its mass are concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus.
Electrons revolve around the nucleus; the atom as a whole is electrically neutral.

items.followUp: Write any four properties of a mixture.

rubric.why: Elements in a compound are chemically combined in a definite proportion.
rubric.description: States that a compound has a fixed composition or ratio of elements.
rubric.how: Award for any equivalent statement about definite proportions.

rubric.why: A compound generally has properties different from those of its constituent elements.
rubric.description: Compares the properties of a compound with those of its elements.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the compound's properties differ from its constituent elements.

rubric.why: A compound can be separated into its elements by chemical means, not by physical methods alone.
rubric.description: States that a compound is decomposed or separated chemically.
rubric.how: Award for a correct statement about chemical decomposition.

rubric.why: A definite formula, fixed melting/boiling point, or homogeneous nature is another valid property.
rubric.description: Gives another correct property of a compound.
rubric.how: Award for any one valid property not already credited.

modelAnswer: A compound contains its elements in a fixed proportion by mass.
Its properties are different from those of its constituent elements.
It can be decomposed into its elements only by chemical means.
It has a definite chemical formula and fixed melting and boiling points.

items.followUp: Explain the formation of an ionic bond between magnesium and oxygen atoms.

rubric.why: A chemical bond is the force of attraction that holds atoms or ions together.
rubric.description: Defines a chemical bond.
rubric.how: Award for a definition based on the attractive force holding particles together.

rubric.why: Sodium has one outer-shell electron and chlorine has seven, enabling electron transfer.
rubric.description: Identifies the relevant outer-shell electron arrangement.
rubric.how: Award for correct configurations or the relevant valence-electron counts.

rubric.why: The ionic bond forms by transfer of sodium's outer electron to chlorine.
rubric.description: Describes the electron transfer.
rubric.how: Award for correctly stating the direction of transfer.

rubric.why: Electron transfer forms oppositely charged sodium and chloride ions.
rubric.description: Identifies the ions formed.
rubric.how: Award for both correct ions and charges.

rubric.why: The electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions forms ionic sodium chloride.
rubric.description: States the attraction that forms the ionic compound and/or its formula.
rubric.how: Award for the ionic attraction or the correctly named/formula compound.

modelAnswer: A chemical bond is the force of attraction that holds atoms or ions together.
A sodium atom has the electronic configuration 2,8,1, and a chlorine atom has 2,8,7.
Sodium transfers its outer electron to chlorine: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻; Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻.
This forms a positive sodium ion (Na⁺) and a negative chloride ion (Cl⁻), each with a stable outer shell.
The electrostatic attraction between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ forms an ionic bond, producing sodium chloride (NaCl).

items.followUp: Define vapour pressure and explain how temperature affects it.

rubric.why: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by the vapour above a liquid.
rubric.description: Defines vapour pressure in terms of pressure exerted by vapour.
rubric.how: Award for the central definition.

rubric.why: The definition applies when vapour is in equilibrium with its liquid, normally in a closed container.
rubric.description: Includes the equilibrium condition or closed-container context.
rubric.how: Award for either qualifying condition.

rubric.why: The question asks specifically about the effect of molecule size.
rubric.description: Identifies the larger-molecule comparison.
rubric.how: Award for explicitly referring to increasing molecular size.

rubric.why: Larger molecules generally have stronger intermolecular attractions, reducing escape into vapour and lowering vapour pressure.
rubric.description: States the direction of the effect and/or its cause.
rubric.how: Award for lower vapour pressure or a correct explanation using stronger attractions/less evaporation.

modelAnswer: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by a vapour in equilibrium with its liquid in a closed container at a given temperature.
As molecular size increases, intermolecular forces generally become stronger.
Fewer molecules escape from the liquid surface, so the vapour pressure decreases.

items.followUp: Compare metals and non-metals with respect to chemical properties.

rubric.why: Metals are generally lustrous, while non-metals are generally dull.
rubric.description: Compares appearance.
rubric.how: Award for the correct contrast in lustre.

rubric.why: Metals can generally be beaten into sheets or drawn into wires; solid non-metals are generally brittle.
rubric.description: Compares malleability, ductility, or brittleness.
rubric.how: Award for a correct contrast.

rubric.why: Metals generally conduct heat and electricity well; non-metals generally conduct poorly.
rubric.description: Compares conductivity.
rubric.how: Award for the correct contrast in heat or electrical conductivity.

rubric.why: Metals generally produce a ringing sound when struck, whereas non-metals are generally non-sonorous.
rubric.description: Compares sonority.
rubric.how: Award for the correct contrast.

modelAnswer: Metals are generally lustrous; non-metals are generally dull.
Metals are malleable and ductile; solid non-metals are generally brittle.
Metals are good conductors of heat and electricity; non-metals are generally poor conductors.
Metals are sonorous; non-metals are generally non-sonorous.
